content: Sore throat, also known as pharyngitis, is characterized by a painful sensation in the posterior region of the throat, which is caused by inflammation of the pharynx. It is one of the most common complaints among patients seeking medical attention from their primary care physicians. In the United States, approximately 12 million outpatient visits annually are attributed to sore throat. The majority of cases are observed in children and adolescents. In most individuals, the underlying cause is an acute, self-limiting viral infection. However, in adults, group A streptococcal (GAS) infection is the most common bacterial etiology for acute pharyngitis. As a physician, it is critical to recognize clinical signs that may indicate life-threatening airway obstruction or deep tissue infections and to address these conditions promptly. Common Causes of Sore Throat: 1. Viral upper respiratory tract infections caused by pathogens such as adenovirus, rhinovirus, coronavirus, enterovirus, influenza A and B, parainfluenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus, and SARS-CoV-2. 2. Group A streptococcal (GAS) infection. 3. Group C and G Streptococcus infections. 4. Arcanobacterium haemolyticum. 5. Fusobacterium necrophorum, which is associated with Lemierre's syndrome. 6. Mycoplasma and Chlamydia species. 7. Corynebacterium diphtheriae. 8. Acute HIV infection. 9. Neisseria gonorrhoeae. 10. Epstein-Barr virus and other herpesviruses, such as cytomegalovirus (CMV) and herpes simplex virus (HSV). 11. Non-infectious causes, including allergic rhinitis, sinusitis, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), smoking, inhalation of dry air (especially in winter), and vocal strain. 12. Medications, such as angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and chemotherapeutic agents. Diagnosis: The diagnostic approach to sore throat in adults involves clinical evaluation and, when indicated, the use of diagnostic tests such as rapid antigen detection tests (RADTs) and throat cultures to confirm or rule out GAS infection. Treatment: The treatment of sore throat in adults should follow evidence-based guidelines, such as those provided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA). Antibiotics: Physicians should prescribe antibiotics judiciously to minimize the risk of adverse reactions and the development of bacterial resistance in the community. Antibiotics should only be administered to patients with a high clinical suspicion of GAS infection or those with positive RADT and throat culture results. Antibiotics can reduce symptom severity, accelerate recovery, and decrease the risk of complications associated with GAS infection. Supportive Therapy: The IDSA recommends the use of aspirin, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), or acetaminophen for pain relief. Randomized clinical trials have demonstrated that NSAIDs are more effective than acetaminophen in alleviating symptoms. Emergency Management: If alarm signs such as stridor, coughing, or drooling are present, physicians should assess for conditions like croup or epiglottitis and provide emergent medical support. Do's: Administer antibiotics with caution and only when clinically indicated. Use supportive therapies, such as NSAIDs or acetaminophen, to manage pain and discomfort. Promptly address any signs of airway obstruction or severe infection. Don'ts: Avoid prescribing oral glucocorticoids as analgesics due to their unfavorable risk-benefit profile. Glucocorticoids should only be considered in patients with significant odynophagia (painful swallowing) and dysphagia (difficulty swallowing).
